archetype.name: Pocket Passer (still developing)
archetype.definition: A second-year, rhythm-based thrower who wins between the hashes at 10-19 yards and is improving his pocket management, but who hasn't yet turned that into a reliable deep game or a functional quick game.

report.headline: Better process, same results: Ward's middle-of-field gains are buried by screens and deep misses.
report.take:
Cam Ward's season looks like a stalled sophomore year: 1-7, 5.98 yards an attempt (39th of 49), a 2.4% touchdown rate that sits 1.8 points under the league average, and -0.075 EPA per dropback (33rd). Look past the totals, though, and the process has moved forward from his rookie year. His completion rate is up 2.7 points, CPOE is up 1.9, bad throws are down 2.3 points, and he's getting the ball out 0.19 seconds faster. The clearest gain is under pressure. His pressure-to-sack rate has dropped from 32.2% last season to 18.6%, 7th-best among 42 qualifiers. He's still pressured more than most, but he's no longer holding the ball into sacks.

What's dragging the numbers is mostly the ends of the route tree, not the middle. On throws of 10-19 air yards he's been very good: +0.443 EPA per attempt, +4.0 CPOE, 25.3 EPA added. On throws behind the line he has given back 16.6 EPA, and on throws of 20+ yards another 15.1, completing 17.4% with a -21.3 CPOE and two interceptions on 23 tries. Some of the behind-the-line problem belongs to the scheme and the back. Targets to Tony Pollard have cost -0.763 EPA apiece, -16 in total, and that one target bucket nearly wipes out everything Carnell Tate has added. The deep misses are on Ward. That's an accuracy problem, not an aggressiveness one, since his intended air yards (6.88) are already short.

Context matters too. This is a run-leaning offense (pass rate over expected -5.4, 26th) paired with a defense ranked 26th, so he's often throwing from behind. Third downs have been ugly, a 30.6% conversion rate, but the average distance is 8.3 yards and his third-down CPOE is neutral. That points to early downs failing more than him failing in the moment. All six of his passing touchdowns came in the red zone, so there's been almost nothing explosive from outside it. The counterweight is late-game play. In close fourth quarters he's at +0.319 EPA per play with a +5.2 CPOE, and his no-huddle work is positive. When the offense is spread out and he's dictating tempo, he plays like a different quarterback.

The recent arc is encouraging but noisy. Over the last three games his EPA per dropback is +0.115, a swing of +0.189 against his season, and his sack rate fell to 3.1%. His aggressiveness ticked up to 16-17% in Weeks 7-8. But that stretch's -6.5 CPOE is dragged down by a 102-yard, -20.1 CPOE outing at Indianapolis. The Week 8 shootout at Cincinnati (304 yards, +8.7 EPA) also came against a 16th-ranked defense in a 45.5 total. He is trending up, but not yet a quarterback who lifts a bad roster.

strengths.title: Intermediate middle-of-field accuracy
strengths.body: His 10-19 yard throws are the engine of every positive drive. He completes them above expectation and has added more EPA there than he's lost anywhere else. That is a repeatable skill tied to timing and processing, and it shows up across directions rather than in one lucky route. It should hold, though it depends on receivers who win at that level.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance has genuinely improved
strengths.body: He's still pressured often, but far fewer of those pressures end in sacks than last year. A quicker release and a 5.0% sack rate (13th) back that up. It comes from him, not just the line, because the line's hit rate hasn't changed his pressure volume. A shift this large from one season to the next usually reflects real development rather than noise.

strengths.title: Plays up in tempo and late
strengths.body: In close fourth quarters and no-huddle he has been efficient and accurate. His legs add value too: scrambles and designed runs both carry clearly positive EPA. Late-game samples are small (46 plays), but together they suggest a quarterback who is better when the structure loosens.

concerns.title: No functioning deep ball
concerns.body: Two interceptions and a 17.4% completion rate on 20+ yard throws, with CPOE more than 21 points under expected. That is misses, not drops or bad luck on contested balls. Twenty-three attempts is a small sample, but with an offense that already lacks explosives, it caps his ceiling until it improves.

concerns.title: Screen and checkdown game is a sinkhole
concerns.body: Throws behind the line convert at a 79.5% rate yet lose heavily, because they go nowhere. Pollard's targets alone account for -16 EPA. This is more a design and personnel issue than a Ward flaw, but it inflates his completion rate while draining his efficiency. Without Tyjae Spears, the backfield options don't get better.

concerns.title: Under-center turnovers and third downs
concerns.body: Four of his five interceptions came on 36 under-center attempts, likely a small-sample spike tied to play-action looks rather than a lasting trait. Third downs are the more durable worry: long distances and a 30.6% conversion rate keep killing drives. That reflects early-down failure across the whole offense.

trend.note: His EPA climbed from a Week 5 low of -16.9 against Houston to +5.9 and +8.7 in Weeks 7-8, and his last-three-game EPA per dropback is well above his season mark. The Indianapolis dud in between, and an accuracy dip in that stretch, keep it from being a clean upswing.

nextGame.headline: Stingiest short-pass defense, no Tate, and a likely trailing script
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville is a bad matchup for how Ward plays. Its defense ranks 3rd in EPA, 3rd against the pass and 3rd against the run, and it is the best in the league on short throws. That is where most of his attempts go. It shuts down tight ends and backs as receivers, so the Helm and Pollard outlets look even worse than usual. The one soft spot is deep, where Jacksonville ranks 27th. That's exactly where Ward has been at his worst, so the opening is only real if his deep accuracy finally shows up. Offenses pass against the Jaguars more than normal, and with Jacksonville's offense ranked 5th and the Titans 10.5-point home underdogs, Ward should get volume from a trailing script. That gives some yardage floor, but against a defense that rarely hands out chunk gains.

Availability cuts against him. Carnell Tate, his most-targeted receiver and the biggest positive EPA contributor in the passing game, is out with a shoulder injury. That pushes more of the load to Ayomanor and Wan'Dale Robinson and leaves a thinner group behind them. Left guard Peter Skoronski (hamstring) and right tackle JC Latham (finger), both full-time starters, left the Cincinnati game questionable to return. Their status after the bye will shape how often Ward is pressured against a front ranked 8th in hit rate. The extra week of rest helps both linemen's chances. Spears is also out, leaving Pollard as the main back against a run defense ranked 3rd.

keyMatchups.title: His short game versus Jacksonville's strength
keyMatchups.body: Most of Ward's attempts travel under 10 yards, and Jacksonville allows the least EPA in the league on short throws. If the Titans lean on quick game and screens, expect long third downs. That's his weakest situation.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a leaky back end
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville ranks 27th against deep passes, the one clear crack in the unit. Ward has completed fewer than one in five of his deep attempts. A couple of hits would change the game; more misses would end drives early.

keyMatchups.title: Life after Tate
keyMatchups.body: With Tate out, the receiver who slides into the third-wideout role draws a spot where Jacksonville has given up a lot to WR3s. Meanwhile the tight end and lead back face the league's stingiest coverage by EPA. Ayomanor's efficient early targets make him the likeliest beneficiary.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Titans let him attack the 10-19 yard window and take deep shots, or retreat into the screen-and-checkdown game that Jacksonville's short-area defense is built to smother.

restOfSeason.body:
The sustainable parts of Ward's game are the improved sack avoidance, his intermediate accuracy and the modest rushing value. Those support a floor near league-average volume: roughly 175 to 215 passing yards a game in a run-leaning offense that will often trail. The touchdown rate should rise a little from its current low, since a quarterback this efficient in the intermediate range rarely stays at 2.4%. The last three games also point to a slightly better version than the season line.

His efficiency won't climb into the positive range for good unless the deep ball and the behind-the-line game stop leaking points. One is his accuracy; the other is the play-calling and backs. The Week 8 shootout should be treated as the top of his range, not the new baseline. Expect EPA per dropback to hover around average to slightly below. Tate's return and the health of Skoronski and Latham are the biggest variables.
swingFactors: Skoronski and Latham's availability on the line

confidence.note: Eight starts with a clear year-over-year process gain, but the recent upswing leans on one shootout, and key splits rest on small samples.
